stories.headline: Inside the House GOP strategy to capitalize on Democrats' warring factions in the new Congress
stories.note: House Republicans have a plan to exploit the Democrats' internal feuds in the new Congress.
body: House Republicans are heading into the new Congress in the minority, but they say they plan to stay on offense against the incoming Democratic majority.

Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, who moves from majority whip to minority whip alongside incoming Minority Leader Jim Jordan, told Fox News Digital the GOP will hold Democrats accountable for the ideas of their far-left wing, even without control over which bills reach the floor.

Emmer said his job will be to coordinate committee hearings and floor votes that "expose and define exactly who these people really are." He also predicted little bipartisanship, saying he doubts Democrats will even be able to work with each other.

Other Republicans outlined tactics: Rep. Randy Fine wants to lean on amendments, and Rep. Nick LaLota pointed to the motion to recommit, which gives the minority a vote to change or kill a bill. LaLota noted that anything a Speaker Jeffries passes still needs President Trump's signature and likely 60 Senate votes.
Why it matters: With Democrats split between their progressive and moderate wings, Republicans see a chance to force tough votes that highlight those divisions ahead of 2028.

stories.headline: 'Traitor!': Jeffries gets rude awakening at Democratic convention as heckler erupts
stories.note: Jeffries' own base turned on him in public, a sign of a fractured Democratic coalition.
body: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become the next House speaker, was repeatedly interrupted by protesters while speaking at a Democratic post-election conference in Denver on Friday.

The hecklers, at a panel moderated by consultant Jessica Tarlov at the "What's Next" conference, demanded to know when Democrats would deliver a Green New Deal and Medicare-for-all. One shouted that Jeffries was a liar, and others said they were young and scared for their future.
The conference bills itself as a major gathering to chart the party's direction through 2028 after Democrats' big gains in the Nov. 3 midterms.

Jeffries' office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. House Democrats vote on their leadership slate Nov. 18, and Jeffries is running unopposed for the speaker nomination.
Why it matters: Even in victory, Democrats' leader is facing open anger from his party's left flank, a preview of the infighting Republicans hope to exploit.

stories.headline: Blue wave meets ballot box surprises as voters split on abortion, voter ID and billionaire taxes
stories.note: Even in a Democratic year, voters didn't buy the whole progressive agenda at the ballot box.
body: Democrats won big on Election Night, but a look at statewide ballot measures shows voters backed several conservative priorities at the same time.

Voters in Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio approved voter ID measures. North Carolina's amendment, extending photo ID to all forms of voting, passed about 60% to 40%; Ohio's Issue 3 passed roughly 65% to 35%; and Nevada's Question 7, creating the state's first voter ID requirement, passed about 62% to 38%.
In Idaho, voters made English the official language in the state constitution by about 63% to 37%. State Rep. Dale Hawkins said a common language helps ensure "our culture will survive."
Idaho voters also rejected Proposition 1, which would have created a right to abortion up to fetal viability, by roughly 56% to 44%.

Why it matters: The results suggest that issues like election integrity and English-language laws remain popular even in a year when Republicans lost ground, giving the GOP a policy foundation to build on.

stories.headline: GOP newcomer who toppled Cory Mills sets sights on fraud, inflation as he heads to Capitol Hill
stories.note: A fresh Republican face heads to Washington focused on kitchen-table issues like inflation and fraud.
body: Florida Republican congressman-elect Ryan Elijah, a former Central Florida sports broadcaster who beat Rep. Cory Mills in the August GOP primary, says he is heading to Washington focused on fraud, consumer protection and inflation.
Elijah told Fox News Digital he wants to target fraud in taxpayer-funded programs, saying it is wasting "so much of our tax dollars," and hopes both parties will join that effort.

He said voters made clear on Election Day that they want inflation to come down and life to get easier. He also backs banning members of Congress from trading stocks and wants a seat on Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, or Transportation and Infrastructure.
Addressing the GOP's loss of Congress, Elijah urged Republicans to stay united and hold the line on the progress they've made.
Why it matters: A fresh Republican face focused on kitchen-table issues like costs and waste is the kind of message the party will need to win back ground.

stories.headline: Democrats seize on midterm wins to push massive minimum wage hikes, but economists see trouble ahead
stories.note: Economists warn the Democrats' big wage-hike push could cost jobs, giving the GOP an economic argument.
body: Fresh off their midterm wins, Democrats are pushing big minimum wage increases, but economists warn the plans could backfire on small businesses and entry-level workers.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has pledged to raise the state's $7.25 minimum wage to $15, an increase of roughly 107%. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is calling for a federal increase, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the federal minimum "certainly needs to be increased."

Tom Savidge of the American Institute for Economic Research told Fox News Digital a one-size-fits-all federal hike would worsen affordability, risking higher prices, fewer hours and fewer jobs, especially for inexperienced workers.
Another economist pointed to Illinois, which phased in a $15 minimum by 2025 but was among the slowest states to recover from the pandemic. Pritzker's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Why it matters: Democrats are making affordability their central promise, and Republicans can argue that wage mandates could drive up costs and cut jobs instead.

stories.headline: Socialist LA mayor's bold homelessness promise ahead of 2028 Olympics hit with reality check: 'Not optimistic'
stories.note: A socialist mayor's big homelessness promise is already meeting skepticism, a cautionary tale for the left.
body: Incoming Los Angeles Mayor Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, has promised to cut the number of people living in tents and encampments by at least half before the 2028 Summer Olympics.

Her plan calls for more shelter, housing and rental assistance, medical teams sent into encampments, unarmed crisis teams for some emergencies, and more oversight of homelessness spending. She has criticized former Mayor Karen Bass' Inside Safe hotel program as costly.

Santa Monica Coalition co-founder John Alle told Fox News Digital he doubts it will work, predicting homeless people will be bused away before the Games and "wander right back" afterward. He said the plan isn't much different from Bass's.
According to the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority's 2026 count, homelessness rose 3.4% in the city, undoing two years of declines.
Why it matters: LA's experiment with a socialist mayor will be tested on the world stage, and skeptics already see the same failed approach to homelessness.

stories.headline: Alito warns against congressional Supreme Court meddling, says some lower court judges 'have gone far astray'
stories.note: Alito pushes back on Democratic plans to meddle with the Supreme Court.
body: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito warned Thursday that Congress has the power to cripple the high court, including by cutting off its funding, according to The Hill.

Speaking at the Federalist Society's Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner, Alito said it is important to preserve judicial independence, warning that without it the Constitution of 1789 "will no longer be the same."
The Constitution protects justices' pay, but Congress controls the court's broader budget.
Alito also said some lower-court judges have issued unjustified orders blocking presidents' policies in recent years, saying they have at times gone "far astray in abuse of their powers."
Why it matters: With Democrats taking Congress, Alito's remarks are a pointed warning against any push to pressure or restructure the Supreme Court.
